title: Factor with a purpose
chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
goal: Break a number into primes, and know when to stop searching for factors.

scenes.visual: Branch two ways through 60 and regroup the same prime tiles at the bottom.
scenes.narration: Whole numbers bigger than one are made by multiplying primes. A prime has exactly two positive factors, one and itself. Take sixty. Split it into six and ten, then split those again. The prime pieces are two, three, two and five.

scenes.visual: Build a second tree for sixty and slide both lists into the same prime row.
scenes.narration: Start another way. Write sixty as four times fifteen. Four gives two twos, and fifteen gives a three and a five. Rearrange the pieces in increasing order and both trees give the same list. That fixed prime factorisation is why we can work with the pieces.

scenes.visual: Open a blank factor rectangle for ninety-one and present the prime test.
scenes.narration: Is ninety-one prime? Decide which small primes you would try first, and think about how far the search needs to go.

scenes.visual: Build a sequence of prime tests for 91, then assemble the seven by thirteen rectangle.
scenes.narration: Ninety-one is odd, so two fails. Its digits add to ten, so three fails. Its last digit is one, so five fails. Try seven. Seven times thirteen equals ninety-one. These two factors show that ninety-one is composite.

scenes.visual: Use a square-root boundary to place both factors. Test 97 with the only relevant primes and show the nonzero remainders.
scenes.narration: If both factors were bigger than the square root, multiplying them would give too much. So a composite number has a prime factor at or below its square root. For ninety-seven that root lies between nine and ten. Try two, three, five and seven. All leave a remainder, so ninety-seven is prime.

scenes.visual: Separate 66 into 2, 3 and 11 and allocate exactly one prime tile into each of three nonempty boxes.
scenes.narration: Three different whole numbers, each bigger than one, multiply to sixty-six. Which numbers are they? Sixty-six has exactly three prime pieces, two, three and eleven. Each of the three numbers needs a piece. Each gets exactly one, so those three primes are the answer.

scenes.visual: Show the factorisation and prime-test routines, then a blank tree rooted at eighty-four.
scenes.narration: Split a number until all its pieces are prime. When you test whether a number is prime, use the small primes up to its square root. One has only one positive factor. In your notebook, write eighty-four as a product of primes.

notebook_exercise: Write 84 as a product of primes.
